name: Machine learning engineer
summary: Machine learning engineer interviews usually combine software engineering (coding and system design) with machine learning: how models are trained, evaluated, deployed and monitored. Candidates commonly report an ML system design round, questions on deep learning or classical models depending on the team, and for newer AI roles, questions on building with large language models, retrieval and evaluation.
rounds: Coding interview, often similar to a software engineer's
Machine learning fundamentals: models, training, evaluation and the maths behind them
ML system design: a recommendation, search or classification system end to end
Project deep dive on a model you trained or shipped
looks_for: Sound ML basics: loss functions, optimisation, regularisation and evaluation
Engineering skill: clean code, data pipelines, serving and testing
Thinking about the whole system: data, training, serving, monitoring and retraining
Trade-offs between accuracy, latency and cost
Rigorous evaluation, both offline and with live users
Honesty about what a model can and can't do

questions.text: Tell me about a model you took from experiment to production. What was harder than you expected?
covers: The problem, the data and the model you chose
What changed on the way to production: latency, data mismatches, scale
How it performs now, and how you know

questions.text: Describe an experiment you believed in that didn't work. What did you do next?
covers: The hypothesis and why it looked promising
How you found out it didn't work, and whether you ruled out a bug first
What you learned and what you tried instead

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to explain a model's limits to a product team that expected more.
covers: What they expected and what the model could actually do
How you showed it with examples or numbers
What you agreed: a narrower scope, a fallback, more data

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found a bug in a training or data pipeline.
covers: How it showed up: metrics too good, too bad or inconsistent between runs
How you traced it
The fix, and the check you added so it couldn't return

questions.text: Walk me through how gradient descent trains a neural network.
covers: A loss function, gradients from backpropagation, and updating the weights
Learning rate, batches and optimisers such as Adam
Signs of trouble: loss not falling, exploding or vanishing gradients

questions.text: How would you design a system that recommends products or videos to users?
covers: Candidate generation, then ranking, and the signals each step uses
Offline metrics, then an online A/B test
New users and new items, freshness, feedback loops, and serving latency

questions.text: How do you serve a model with low latency at high traffic?
covers: Batch versus real-time predictions, and which the product needs
Smaller or quantised models, caching, and batching requests
Monitoring latency, and a fallback if the model is slow or down

questions.text: A model performs well offline but worse once it's live. What could explain it?
covers: Features computed differently in training and in serving
Training data that included information not known at prediction time
Shifts in the data or feedback effects, and how you'd check each

questions.text: What would you monitor for a model in production?
covers: Input data distributions and missing features
Prediction distributions and, once labels arrive, live accuracy
Latency, errors and cost, with alerts and a plan for retraining

questions.text: Explain regularisation. How do L1, L2 and dropout differ?
covers: Penalising complexity to reduce overfitting
L1 pushes some weights to exactly zero; L2 shrinks all weights
Dropout in neural networks, and when each helps

questions.text: How do transformers handle sequences, and why did they replace recurrent networks for most language tasks?
covers: Attention, letting each token look directly at every other token
Training in parallel instead of step by step
The cost: compute and memory grow quickly with sequence length

questions.text: How would you build an assistant that answers questions from a company's internal documents using a large language model?
covers: Retrieval: splitting documents, embeddings, a vector index and ranking
Putting the retrieved text in the prompt, citing sources, and saying 'I don't know' when unsure
Evaluating answers, and making sure people only see documents they're allowed to

questions.text: How would you evaluate a generative model's outputs when there's no single right answer?
covers: A test set of realistic cases with clear criteria for a good answer
Human review, automated checks, and model-based grading used with care
Tracking failures such as made-up facts or unsafe output across versions

questions.text: How do you make training experiments reproducible?
covers: Versioning code, data and configuration together
Fixed random seeds and recorded environments
Experiment tracking and saved model artefacts

questions.text: You have very little labelled data for a new classification task. What are your options?
covers: Fine-tuning a pre-trained model, or transfer learning
Labelling more data cleverly: active learning, weak labels
Data augmentation, and a simple baseline to compare against

questions.text: Why machine learning engineering rather than research or data science?
covers: Enjoying building models that run reliably for real users
An example from your work or projects that shows it
The balance of engineering and modelling you want

questions.text: Which recent development in AI interests you most, and how might it be useful in our product?
covers: A specific development, explained in plain words
A realistic use in the company's product
Its risks, and how you'd test it before relying on it

tips: Prepare to code like a software engineer; many ML loops include a standard coding round.
Structure ML design answers: problem and metric, data, model, serving, monitoring. Saying the structure first helps the interviewer follow.
Know the maths behind what you claim; be ready to explain backpropagation or a loss function from scratch.
For each project, know the baseline, the metric and the gain over the baseline; a bare accuracy figure invites hard follow-ups.
If you've built with large language models, be ready to say how you evaluated the results, not just which models you used.
